title: The Federal Reserve Explained: Who Really Controls Interest Rates
sources: Federal Reserve press release, Sept 16, 2026: FOMC raised the federal funds target range by 1/4 point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, vote 12-0, first hike since July 2023; interest on reserve balances raised to 3.90% (effective Sept 17, 2026)

Federal Reserve: FOMC has 12 voting members and holds 8 scheduled meetings per year; Board of Governors has 7 members; 12 regional Reserve Banks; dual mandate (maximum employment, stable prices); 2% inflation goal
Federal Reserve History, 'The Meeting at Jekyll Island': Nov 1910, six men (Aldrich, Andrew, Davison, Shelton, Vanderlip, Warburg), duck-hunting cover story, first names only
Federal Reserve History: Panic of 1907 and J.P. Morgan; Federal Reserve Act signed by President Woodrow Wilson, Dec 23, 1913

Federal Reserve: 11 rate increases from March 2022 (0-0.25%) to July 2023 (5.25-5.50%); cuts 2024-2025 to 3.50-3.75% (Dec 10, 2025)
Freddie Mac PMMS: 30-year fixed averaged 7.03% on Sept 24, 2026 (2026 high); Jan 2022 ~3.2% vs Oct 2022 ~7%
Federal Reserve G.19: credit card rate, accounts assessed interest ≈ 22% (2026)

beats.text: Dave just got a letter. His credit card interest rate is going up. And his savings account? It suddenly pays a little more.
Nobody at his bank really decided this. The decision came from a meeting of twelve people in Washington.
On September sixteenth, twenty twenty six, they raised one number by a quarter of a percent. And it rippled into loans all over America.
That group is the Federal Reserve. And it may have more power over Dave's wallet than his boss does.
And the whole thing started with a fake duck hunting trip.
Today: what the Fed is, how one interest rate hits your cards, your mortgage and your savings, what printing money really means, and who should control it.
So what is the Federal Reserve? Short name: the Fed.
It's America's central bank. Think of it as the bank for banks. Dave can't open an account there. But Dave's bank can.
It has three big parts. A board of seven governors in Washington. Twelve regional Fed banks around the country. And a committee that sets interest rates.
That committee has twelve voting members. They meet eight times a year. And the whole world watches.
Congress gave the Fed two jobs. Keep prices stable. And help as many people as possible find jobs.
Stable prices has a number. The Fed wants inflation around two percent a year. Not zero. Just a gentle, boring two.
Think of the Fed as the thermostat of the economy. Too hot, it cools things down. Too cold, it warms things up.
But why does America even have one? Let's go back to nineteen oh seven.
Back then, there was no central bank. Panic spread. People lined up to pull their money out, and banks started to fail.
Remember the bank run from our very first video? Now picture that all over the country, with nobody to step in.
One rich banker, J P Morgan, personally helped stop the panic. And everyone agreed: one rich guy can't be the plan next time.
So in November nineteen ten, six powerful men boarded a secret train to Jekyll Island, off the coast of Georgia.
Their cover story? They were going duck hunting. They used only their first names, so nobody would know who they were.
Our duck would like everyone to know he was not consulted.
The plan they wrote became the base for the Federal Reserve Act. President Woodrow Wilson signed it in December nineteen thirteen. And the Fed was born.
So how does the Fed actually control interest rates? With one special number.
It's called the federal funds rate. It's the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.
Every night, some banks have extra cash, and some are short. So they lend to each other. Just for one night.

The Fed sets a target for that rate. And its main trick is simple. It pays banks interest on money they park at the Fed. Right now, three point nine percent. So why would any bank lend it out for less?
Think of it as the master dial. Turn it up, and money gets more expensive everywhere. Turn it down, and money gets cheaper.
So where is the dial now? On September sixteenth, the Fed raised it to a range of three point seven five to four percent.
It was the first hike since twenty twenty three. The vote was twelve to zero. The reason? Inflation is still too high. In August, prices were up three point four percent from a year earlier.
So how does a rate for overnight bank loans end up in Dave's wallet? Throw a stone in a pond.
The stone is the Fed. The first ripple hits the banks. Their borrowing costs go up.
The next ripple hits Dave's credit card. Most card rates are variable, so they follow the Fed, often within a month or two. And cards already charge around twenty two percent. Remember the raccoon?
Then the ripple reaches car loans, business loans, and mortgages.

Mortgages are a bit different. They follow long term rates, which move on what investors expect the Fed to do. This week, the average thirty year mortgage rate hit about seven percent. The highest this year.

Here's why that matters. On a three hundred thousand dollar mortgage, a three percent rate costs about twelve hundred and sixty five dollars a month. At seven percent? About two thousand. Same house. Over seven hundred dollars more, every single month.
But the ripple has a good side too. When rates go up, savings accounts can pay more. Grandma, with her cash in the bank, is finally smiling.
Higher rates: borrowing hurts, saving helps. Lower rates: the opposite. It's a seesaw.
Now, why would the Fed ever want to make loans more expensive? Let's go back to twenty twenty two.
After the pandemic, prices went wild. In June twenty twenty two, inflation hit nine point one percent. The highest in about forty years.
Remember the bread in a town from our inflation video? Too much money chasing too few things. So prices go up.
So the Fed grabbed the dial. In March twenty twenty two, the rate was almost zero. By July twenty twenty three, eleven hikes later, it was over five percent.
One of the fastest jumps in decades. Like cooling an overheated kitchen by opening every window at once.
It hurt. Mortgage rates more than doubled. Home sales slowed. And some banks that had bet on low rates got into trouble. Like Silicon Valley Bank, from our first video.
But inflation came down. Not all the way to two percent. But a long way down from nine.
Most people think the Fed can just switch inflation off. Nope. Rate changes can take a year or more to fully work. It's like steering a giant ship, not a bicycle.
Now, the famous money printer. Is the Fed really printing money?
Remember the duck from our very first video? When a bank makes a loan, it creates new money. Like drawing a duck on paper, and it comes to life.
The Fed has an even bigger pen. When rates are already near zero and the economy still needs help, it uses a tool called quantitative easing. Q E.
It means the Fed buys huge amounts of bonds, mostly government bonds and mortgage bonds. And it pays with brand new money, created on a computer.
Here's the myth bust. There's no giant printer. Paper cash is printed by the Treasury. The Fed mostly creates digital money for banks, called reserves.
But the effect is real. Before two thousand eight, the Fed held about nine hundred billion dollars of assets. By April twenty twenty two, almost nine trillion. Ten times bigger.
Since then, it has done the reverse. Quantitative tightening. Letting bonds expire, so that money quietly disappears. Today, it's around six point seven trillion.
So yes, the Fed can make ducks. Very big ducks. And it can make them disappear too.
Which brings us to the big fight. Who should control this power?
The Fed is designed to be independent. The president picks the chair and the governors. The Senate approves them. But after that, the president can't just order a rate cut.
In May twenty twenty six, Kevin Warsh became the new chair, replacing Jerome Powell. And the old debate got loud again.
Side one says independence is essential. Politicians love low rates before elections. Loans feel cheap, people feel rich. And the inflation bill arrives later.

It has happened before. In the early nineteen seventies, White House tapes show President Nixon pushing his Fed chair for easy money. Many economists say it helped fuel the big inflation that followed.

Side two says the Fed has enormous power, and its leaders are not elected. Some argue it should answer more to voters and to Congress. And it makes mistakes too, like calling inflation temporary in twenty twenty one.
Both sides want stable prices and good jobs. They disagree on who should hold the dial. That's a political question. But now you know how the dial works.
So Dave can't control the Fed. But he can control how it hits him. Education, not advice.
One. Know which debts are variable. Credit cards and some loans move with the Fed. Paying those down first protects Dave when rates rise.
Two. When rates are high, make savings work. Compare savings accounts. Some pay far more than others, for the same insured safety.
Three. For big loans, understand fixed versus variable. A fixed rate mortgage stays the same, even if the Fed hikes ten times.
Four. Don't try to outsmart the Fed. Even professionals get surprised. Build a plan that works whether rates go up or down.
And five. Glance at the headlines after the eight meetings a year. Five minutes of reading can save Dave a lot of surprises.
So let's recap.
One. The Fed is America's central bank. It was born in nineteen thirteen, after a secret meeting disguised as a duck hunt.
Two. It sets one master rate, and that ripples into credit cards, mortgages, and savings.
Three. It can create money on a computer. And who should control that power is a real debate.
Next time, Dave walks into a casino. The lights. The free drinks. The jackpot sounds. And he finds out how casinos always win.
Subscribe. Unlike the Fed, you don't need a secret duck hunt to join.
